drills.q: What's the fundamental structural difference between a B+Tree and an LSM-Tree?
drills.a: B+Tree updates in place, staying sorted on disk always, paying reorganization cost (splits) per write. LSM-Tree never updates in place — writes buffer in a memtable, flush as immutable SSTables, and background compaction merges them, deferring reorganization off the write path.

drills.q: Derive B-Tree height for 100M rows with fanout 680.
drills.a: height = log_680(100,000,000) ≈ 3. With top levels cache-resident, a warm lookup is typically 1-2 real disk I/Os despite the log N framing.

drills.q: Define write, read, and space amplification with typical numbers for each engine family.
drills.a: WA = physical/logical bytes written, RA = disk reads per logical read, SA = physical/logical live bytes on disk. B-Tree: WA ~3-4x, RA ~1-2x, SA ~1.1-1.5x. LSM leveled: WA ~20-30x+, RA ~1-2x tuned / 5-10x+ untuned, SA ~1.1-1.3x tuned, spikes to 2x+ mid-compaction.

drills.q: Size-tiered vs leveled compaction: what's the actual tradeoff, and which minimizes what?
drills.a: Size-tiered: lower write amplification (~10-15x), but overlapping key ranges across files raise read amplification and space can spike toward 2x mid-merge. Leveled: higher write amplification (~20-30x+, data rewritten roughly once per level), but non-overlapping key ranges per level give lower read amplification and tighter space usage.

drills.q: Mechanically, what causes B-Tree write amplification vs LSM write amplification?
drills.a: B-Tree: one row update dirties a whole page (8-16KB), and the whole page flushes even though only a fraction logically changed; splits double this. LSM: a key gets physically rewritten roughly once per compaction pass, and the number of passes it survives grows with the number of levels the dataset has grown into.

drills.q: An LSM-backed store's read latency has been climbing for two weeks. What do you check first, and why not add an index?
drills.a: Check compaction metrics first: L0 file count and pending-compaction-bytes. Compaction has almost certainly fallen behind write throughput, so more files must be checked per read. Adding an index is a red flag here — the read path already uses the LSM's sorted structure and bloom filters; this is an operational compaction-debt problem on the write/background side.

drills.q: What does a bloom filter buy an LSM-Tree, with real numbers, and what happens under memory pressure?
drills.a: It gives a fast 'definitely not present / maybe present' check per SSTable; RocksDB's default ~10 bits/key yields ~1% false-positive rate, skipping disk reads on ~99% of files that don't contain the key. Under memory pressure, bloom filters can get evicted from cache, forcing a real disk read just to check membership — a common cause of latency regressions after a memory-limit change.

drills.q: State the RUM conjecture and explain why you can't minimize write, read, and space amplification simultaneously.
drills.a: Read, Update, Memory(space) amplification form a proven tradeoff triangle: optimizing any two makes the third worse. B-Trees optimize read and space at the cost of update cost; LSM-Trees optimize update cost at the cost of read and space — neither is a strict improvement, they occupy different points on the curve.

drills.q: Design the compaction strategy for a metrics/time-series system with 30-day uniform TTL retention.
drills.a: Time-Window Compaction Strategy: bucket SSTables by write-time window, compact only within a window, never merge across windows. When a window's TTL fully expires, drop the entire file(s) rather than rewriting to remove a few expired keys — turns expiry into a cheap file delete instead of a rewrite.

drills.q: Why does an LSM sometimes need close to 2x the dataset's logical size in disk space mid-operation?
drills.a: During a compaction (especially full/major compaction), the input SSTables and the newly-written merged output file coexist on disk until the merge finishes and inputs are deleted, temporarily requiring close to double the steady-state footprint. This must be planned for in disk provisioning, not just steady-state size.

drills.q: When would you choose Cassandra/RocksDB over Postgres, and what's the mistake version of that choice?
drills.a: Choose LSM-backed storage when sustained write throughput is the primary constraint and reads are less latency-sensitive or served through a separate cache/index. It's a mistake when the workload needs multi-row ACID transactions, complex joins, or is read-dominated with unpredictable access patterns — Postgres's B-Tree plus mature planner and transactions wins there.

drills.q: Why does B-Tree lookup cost stay roughly constant as data grows, while LSM write amplification grows with data size?
drills.a: B-Tree height (log_fanout(N)) grows extremely slowly with N at typical fanouts (~680), so per-write page touches stay roughly constant. LSM levels grow (each ~10x the last) as data volume grows, and a surviving key is rewritten roughly once per level it passes through, so total write amplification for long-lived keys scales with the number of levels.
